rules: Both `enum` and `const` are ALWAYS applied, with no gating on instance type, and each yields AT MOST 1 error. `{"enum":[1],"const":1}` + instance true => 2. `{"const":2,"type":"string"}` + instance 1 => 2. `{"const":1,"type":"string"}` + instance 1 => 1.

const: emit 1 error iff NOT equal(instance, const). enum: emit 1 error iff equal(x, instance) is false for EVERY x obtained by iterating `enums`. Both keywords use the SAME strict recursive equality relation (there is no laxer path for enum): `[1]` vs `{"enum":[[true]]}` => 1, exactly like `{"const":[true]}` => 1.

EQUALITY DECISION PROCEDURE equal(a,b): (1) if a and b are the same NaN => true (see NaN rule); (2) if either is a string => equal iff both are strings with identical code points; (3) if both are arrays => equal iff same length AND equal() pairwise in order; (4) if both are objects => equal iff same key count AND every key of a exists in b with equal() values; (5) otherwise => bool-vs-number is NEVER equal (true!=1, false!=0, both directions, any depth), null equals only null, and number-vs-number uses EXACT mathematical value comparison (Python int is arbitrary precision).
Numbers: 1 vs 1.0, 1.0 vs 1, 1e2 vs 100, 100 vs 1e2, 100.0 vs 100 all => 0 errors. -0.0 vs 0 and 0 vs -0.0 => 0 errors (signed zero is equal, in const and enum, and nested: [-0.0] vs const [0] => 0).

Booleans are a distinct type at every depth: 1/{"const":true} => 1, true/{"const":1} => 1, 0/{"const":false} => 1, false/{"const":0} => 1, 1.0/{"const":true} => 1, 0.0/{"const":false} => 1, -0.0/{"const":false} => 1, 1/{"enum":[true]} => 1, true/{"enum":[1]} => 1, 0/{"enum":[false]} => 1, false/{"enum":[0]} => 1, [1]/{"const":[true]} => 1, [true]/{"const":[1]} => 1, [1]/{"enum":[[true]]} => 1, [true]/{"enum":[[1]]} => 1, [[1]]/{"const":[[true]]} => 1, {"a":1}/{"const":{"a":true}} => 1, {"a":true}/{"enum":[{"a":1}]} => 1, {"a":{"b":{"c":1}}}/{"const":{"a":{"b":{"c":true}}}} => 1, [0]/{"enum":[[false]]} => 1, [false]/{"const":[0]} => 1. Matching booleans => 0 (true/{"const":true}, false/{"const":false}, [[true]]/{"enum":[[[true]]]}).

NaN COMPARES EQUAL TO NaN here (the reference's JSON parser hands out one shared NaN object and equality short-circuits on identity): NaN/{"const":NaN} => 0, NaN/{"enum":[NaN]} => 0, NaN/{"enum":[1,NaN]} => 0, [NaN]/{"const":[NaN]} => 0, [NaN]/{"enum":[[NaN]]} => 0, {"a":NaN}/{"const":{"a":NaN}} => 0, {"a":[NaN,Infinity]}/{"const":{"a":[NaN,Infinity]}} => 0. NaN vs a number is unequal: NaN/{"const":1} => 1, 1/{"const":NaN} => 1, [NaN]/{"const":[1]} => 1.

Infinities: 1e400 overflows to +inf, so 1e400/{"const":1e400} => 0, Infinity/{"const":1e400} => 0, Infinity/{"enum":[Infinity]} => 0, 1e400/{"const":-1e400} => 1, -Infinity/{"const":Infinity} => 1, -Infinity/{"const":-Infinity} => 0.

Strings only ever equal strings, byte-for-byte code point identical; there is NO substring, NO number/bool coercion, NO unicode normalization, NO case folding: "1"/{"const":1} => 1, 1/{"const":"1"} => 1, "true"/{"const":true} => 1, true/{"enum":["true","True",1]} => 1, "a"/{"const":"A"} => 1, "é"/{"const":"é"} => 1, "Å"/{"const":"Å"} => 1, "é"/{"const":"é"} => 0, "😀"/{"const":"😀"} => 0, "\ud800"/{"const":"\ud800"} => 0, "\ud800"/{"const":"\udfff"} => 1, "a�b"/{"const":"a�b"} => 0, "a�b"/{"const":"ab"} => 1, "1"/{"enum":[1,1.0,true,"1 "]} => 1, ["1"]/{"const":[1]} => 1.
A string is NOT array-like for equality purposes: "ab"/{"const":["a","b"]} => 1 and ["a","b"]/{"const":"ab"} => 1.

Objects: key ORDER is irrelevant, key SET must match exactly. {"a":1,"b":2}/{"const":{"b":2,"a":1}} => 0, {"b":{"y":2,"x":1}}/{"const":{"b":{"x":1,"y":2}}} => 0, {"a":1,"b":2}/{"const":{"a":1}} => 1 (extra key), {"a":1}/{"const":{"a":1,"b":2}} => 1 (missing key), {"a":1}/{"const":{"b":1}} => 1 (same size, different names), {"A":1}/{"const":{"a":1}} => 1 (case-sensitive keys), {"é":1}/{"const":{"é":1}} => 1 (no key normalization), {"1":2}/{"const":{"1":2.0}} => 0 (values still numeric-equal).
Duplicate keys in the JSON source: LAST occurrence wins, on both instance and schema side. {"a":1,"a":2}/{"const":{"a":2}} => 0 and {"a":2}/{"const":{"a":1,"a":2}} => 0.

Arrays and objects are never equal to each other, even when empty: []/{"const":{}} => 1, {}/{"const":[]} => 1, [[]]/{"const":[{}]} => 1, {"a":{}}/{"const":{"a":[]}} => 1. {}/{"const":{}} => 0, []/{"enum":[{},[],""]} => 0. Scalars never equal containers: 1/{"const":[]} => 1, 1/{"const":{}} => 1, 1/{"enum":[[1],[[1]],{"1":1}]} => 1.

null equals only null: null/{"const":null} => 0, null/{"enum":[null]} => 0, null/{"const":false} => 1, null/{"const":0} => 1, null/{"const":""} => 1, null/{"const":[]} => 1, null/{"enum":[false,0,"",[],{}]} => 1, [null]/{"const":[false]} => 1, {"a":null}/{"const":{"a":null}} => 0. ""/{"const":null} => 1, ""/{"const":0} => 1, ""/{"const":false} => 1, ""/{"const":""} => 0.

enum:[] yields exactly 1 error for ANY instance (1 => 1, null => 1). Duplicate enum members are harmless: 1/{"enum":[2,1,2]} => 0, 1/{"enum":[1,1,1]} => 0. Many mismatching members still produce only 1 error: 1/{"enum":[2,3,4,5,6]} => 1.

`enum` does not have to be an array — its value is merely ITERATED. If enum is a STRING it iterates single characters: "a"/{"enum":"abc"} => 0, "ab"/{"enum":"abc"} => 1 (no substring match), "x"/{"enum":"abc"} => 1, 1/{"enum":"abc"} => 1. If enum is an OBJECT it iterates KEYS: "a"/{"enum":{"a":1,"b":2}} => 0, 1/{"enum":{"a":1}} => 1, 1/{"enum":{}} => 1.

A non-iterable `enum` value (number, boolean, null) raises TypeError => exit 1 with EMPTY stdout: {"enum":5}, {"enum":1}, {"enum":true}, {"enum":null} all crash (stderr `TypeError: 'int'/'bool'/'NoneType' object is not iterable`). The crash happens while draining all errors, so it wins over other keywords' errors: 1/{"const":2,"enum":5} => exit 1, 1/{"type":"string","enum":5} => exit 1.

Nested occurrences each contribute their own top-level error: {"a":2,"b":3}/{"properties":{"a":{"const":1},"b":{"enum":[2]}}} => 2; [1,2]/{"items":{"const":1}} => 1; [2,3]/{"items":{"const":1}} => 2; {"a":1}/{"const":{"a":true},"enum":[{"a":true}]} => 2. Applicators collapse: 1/{"not":{"const":1}} => 1, 1/{"anyOf":[{"const":2},{"const":3}]} => 1.
Draft-07 `$ref` suppresses sibling keywords: 1/{"$ref":"#/definitions/x","enum":[2],"definitions":{"x":true}} => 0. Boolean schemas: 1/true => 0, 1/false => 1.
gotchas: JSON.parse cannot even read the reference's inputs: Python's json accepts the bare literals NaN, Infinity, -Infinity (top-level and nested). You must extend your parser to accept them. Cases: a=NaN b={"const":NaN}; a=Infinity b={"enum":[Infinity]}; a={"a":[NaN,Infinity]} b={"const":{"a":[NaN,Infinity]}} (all => 0).

NaN === NaN is false in JS but the reference treats NaN as EQUAL to NaN (identity short-circuit on the shared parsed NaN object). Your number comparison must be `a === b || (Number.isNaN(a) && Number.isNaN(b))`. Proof: a=NaN b={"const":NaN} => 0; a=[NaN] b={"const":[NaN]} => 0.

Do NOT reach for Object.is as the 'strict' comparator — it would fix NaN but break signed zero. -0.0 vs 0 IS equal here: a=-0.0 b={"const":0} => 0, a=0 b={"const":-0.0} => 0, a=[-0.0] b={"const":[0]} => 0. Object.is(-0,0) === false, so you need the `===`-plus-NaN formula, not Object.is and not a naive deepEqual.

Integer identity beyond 2^53: Python compares integers exactly, JS Number collapses them. a=9007199254740993 b={"const":9007199254740992} => 1 error, but with Number both parse to 9007199254740992 and you would report 0. Same for a=12345678901234567890 b={"const":12345678901234567891} => 1 and a=[9007199254740993] b={"const":[9007199254740992]} => 1. You must retain the literal digits (BigInt) for integer tokens outside the safe range on BOTH the instance and the schema side.

int-vs-float exactness: a=100000000000000000000000 b={"const":1e23} => 1 error (10**23 != the double 1e23), and reversed a=1e23 b={"const":100000000000000000000000} => 1, and a=100000000000000000000000 b={"enum":[1e23]} => 1. But a=10000000000000000000000 b={"const":1e22} => 0 because 1e22 is exactly 10**22. So the rule is exact-rational comparison of BigInt vs double, not 'all big numbers differ'. In plain JS every one of these is 0.

Number vs boolean is never equal, at any depth, and JS loose comparison / a hand-rolled deepEqual using == would get it wrong. a=1 b={"const":true} => 1, a=[1] b={"enum":[[true]]} => 1, a={"a":{"b":{"c":1}}} b={"const":{"a":{"b":{"c":true}}}} => 1, a=[0] b={"enum":[[false]]} => 1. Also beware: JSON.stringify-based comparison would call 1 and true different (fine) but would break key order (see below).

Do NOT implement equality by comparing JSON.stringify output: object key order is irrelevant to the reference. a={"a":1,"b":2} b={"const":{"b":2,"a":1}} => 0 and a={"b":{"y":2,"x":1}} b={"const":{"b":{"x":1,"y":2}}} => 0, while stringify would differ. Stringify also erases 1 vs 1.0 (harmless, they are equal) but cannot represent NaN/Infinity at all.

In Python `str` is a Sequence, yet the reference checks strings FIRST, so a string never structurally matches an array of its characters: a="ab" b={"const":["a","b"]} => 1 and a=["a","b"] b={"const":"ab"} => 1. Don't let a generic 'iterable' path in JS produce a match either.

`enum` is iterated, not indexed, so non-array enum values are legal and behave surprisingly. A string enum iterates characters: a="a" b={"enum":"abc"} => 0 but a="ab" b={"enum":"abc"} => 1 (JS `for (const x of "abc")` matches this). An OBJECT enum iterates its KEYS: a="a" b={"enum":{"a":1,"b":2}} => 0, a=1 b={"enum":{"a":1}} => 1, a=1 b={"enum":{}} => 1 — in JS `for...of` over a plain object THROWS, so you must special-case objects to Object.keys().

Non-iterable enum values must CRASH (exit nonzero, empty stdout), not be treated as a single-member enum or as a no-op: {"enum":5}, {"enum":1}, {"enum":true}, {"enum":null} with a=1 all exit 1. And the crash must win over already-collected errors because the reference materializes the whole error list: a=1 b={"const":2,"enum":5} => exit 1 (not '1'), a=1 b={"type":"string","enum":5} => exit 1.

No Unicode normalization anywhere, including object keys — compare code points/units directly: a="é" b={"const":"é"} => 1, a={"é":1} b={"const":{"é":1}} => 1, a="Å" b={"const":"Å"} => 1. Do not call normalize() or localeCompare. Lone surrogates round-trip and compare fine (a="\ud800" b={"const":"\ud800"} => 0), and embedded NUL is significant (a="a�b" b={"const":"ab"} => 1).

Arrays and objects are in disjoint equality universes even when empty; a JS deepEqual that treats [] and {} as 'both objects with zero own keys' would wrongly return equal. a=[] b={"const":{}} => 1, a={} b={"const":[]} => 1, a=[[]] b={"const":[{}]} => 1, a={"a":{}} b={"const":{"a":[]}} => 1.

Object equality requires equal key COUNT plus every key present — so extra keys on either side fail, and you cannot short-circuit on 'all of const's keys matched': a={"a":1,"b":2} b={"const":{"a":1}} => 1 and a={"a":1} b={"const":{"a":1,"b":2}} => 1.

Duplicate keys in the raw JSON text: last one wins on both sides (a={"a":1,"a":2} b={"const":{"a":2}} => 0; a={"a":2} b={"const":{"a":1,"a":2}} => 0) — matches JSON.parse, so no special work, but do not error on duplicates.

CLI artifact, not semantics: passing a value that starts with '-' as a separate argv token makes argparse treat it as a flag. `--a -Infinity --b '{"const":Infinity}'` exits 2; `--a=-Infinity ...` works and yields 1. Negative plain numbers behave the same way (`--a=-1` works). Use the `--a=VALUE` form when reproducing negative-number cases.
exceptionCases: --a '1' --b '{"enum":5}'  => exit 1, empty stdout, stderr: TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable
--a '1' --b '{"enum":1}'  => exit 1 (even though 1 'equals' the enum value; the value is iterated, not compared)
--a '1' --b '{"enum":true}'  => exit 1, stderr: TypeError: 'bool' object is not iterable
--a '1' --b '{"enum":null}'  => exit 1, stderr: TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable
--a '1' --b '{"const":2,"enum":5}'  => exit 1 (TypeError wins over the const error; nothing is printed)
--a '1' --b '{"type":"string","enum":5}'  => exit 1 (TypeError raised while draining the generator, after a type error was already produced)
--a '1' (missing --b)  => exit 2, argparse usage error: 'the following arguments are required: --b'
--a -Infinity --b '{"const":Infinity}'  => exit 2, argparse treats -Infinity as an unknown option; use --a=-Infinity instead (which returns 1)

rules: CORE RULE: the printed number is the count of errors yielded by the ROOT validator's iter_errors, which is the SUM over root-level keywords of the errors each yields. Pass-through keywords recursively descend and re-yield every child error individually; collapsing keywords yield at most a fixed number of errors regardless of subtree size. There is no dedupe, no cap, no merge, and no ordering effect.

PASSES THROUGH (child errors surface 1:1 at the top level, additively): properties, patternProperties, additionalProperties-as-schema, items-as-schema, items-as-tuple, additionalItems-as-schema, propertyNames, dependencies-as-schema, allOf, if/then, if/else, $ref (incl. definitions), and boolean-false subschemas positioned under any of these.
COLLAPSES TO EXACTLY 1 (subtree errors discarded): anyOf, oneOf, not, contains, additionalProperties:false, additionalItems:false, uniqueItems:true, enum, const. Each yields 0 or 1, never more.
properties: {"a":{"b":1}} vs {properties:{a:{properties:{b:{type:string}},required:[z,y]}}} => 3 (1 nested type + 2 required).
5-level props>props>items>props>allOf>props with one failure per level and 2 at the leaf => 7 (exact sum of leaves; no amplification).
6-level props>items>props>allOf>props>items over 2 array elements => 8 ((2 items x 2 errs + 1 required) + (1 item x 2 errs + 1 required)).
4 nested levels of items down to a single leaf with 2 failures => 2.
allOf yields the concatenation of every branch's errors: 3 branches x 2 failures = 6; nested allOf 3 deep still => 2; empty allOf => 0.
NO DEDUPE: {} vs {allOf:[{required:[a]},{required:[a]}]} => 2 (byte-identical errors both counted).
required yields ONE error PER missing property name: {} vs 25 required names => 25.
dependencies array form yields ONE error per missing dependency: {"a":1} vs {dependencies:{a:[x,y,z]}} => 3.

dependencies schema form passes through, and multiple dependency keys each contribute: {"a":1,"b":1} vs {dependencies:{a:{properties:{b:{type:string,minimum:9}},required:[q]},b:{required:[r,s]}}} => 5.

propertyNames passes through and is applied ONCE PER PROPERTY NAME: {"aaa":1,"bbb":2} vs {propertyNames:{maxLength:2,pattern:'^z'}} => 4 (2 errors x 2 names). A collapsing construct inside propertyNames collapses per name: {propertyNames:{not:{type:string},anyOf:[{minLength:9}]}} on 2 keys => 4.

properties and patternProperties BOTH apply to the same key, and every matching pattern applies: {"ab":1} vs {patternProperties:{'^a':{type:string},'b$':{type:null},'^ab$':{minimum:9}}} => 3. {"ab":1} vs {properties:{ab:{type:string}},patternProperties:{'^a':{type:null}},additionalProperties:false} => 2 (a key matched by properties or patternProperties is NOT 'additional').

items tuple form: only indices present in the instance are validated. [1,2,3] vs items:[5 x {type:string}] => 3. [1,2,3] vs {items:[{type:string}],additionalItems:{type:string,minimum:9}} => 5 (1 + 2 items x 2).
additionalItems is IGNORED when items is a schema (not an array): [1,2] vs {contains:{type:string},items:{type:string},uniqueItems:true,additionalItems:false} => 3.
if/then/else: the `if` subschema's own errors are NEVER reported. if fails and no else => 0. if passes => all `then` errors pass through (=> 3). if fails => all `else` errors pass through (=> 3).

$ref passes through the resolved subschema's errors additively, and the SAME $ref reached N times is counted N times: {"x":1,"y":1} vs properties.x/$ref==properties.y/$ref=={type:string,minLength:3,enum:[q]} => 4 (2 each). Reaching one definition 3 times at 2 different depths => 6. {allOf:[{$ref:d},{$ref:d}]} with d={type:string,minimum:9} => 4.

anyOf/oneOf collapse arbitrarily large subtrees: a subschema that alone yields 60 errors (30 ints vs items{type:string,minimum:9}) yields 1 when wrapped in anyOf; with a sibling minItems:99 the total is 2.
anyOf with 3 failing branches => 1; nested anyOf => 1; empty anyOf => 1; empty oneOf => 1; oneOf with 0 matches => 1; oneOf with 2 matches => 1; oneOf with exactly 1 match => 0.
not: if the subschema SUCCEEDS => exactly 1 error; if the subschema FAILS => 0 (its subtree errors are thrown away). Works the same nested under properties.
contains: 1 error if no element validates (including on an empty array), 0 if any element validates. All per-element failures are discarded.

additionalProperties:false yields exactly 1 error no matter how many extra properties (3 extras => 1). additionalItems:false yields exactly 1 no matter how many extra items ([1..10] with items:[] => 1). uniqueItems:true yields exactly 1 (3 duplicate pairs => 1; 20 identical items => 1).
enum and const each yield at most 1 error regardless of value size; both together => 2. Empty enum ([]) => 1. Under items they contribute per item: [1,2,3] vs {items:{enum:[a],const:b}} => 6.

Boolean schemas: root `true` => 0, root `false` => 1. `false` as a per-item items schema is NOT collapsed: [1,2,3] vs {items:false} => 3; {items:[false,false]} on [1,2,3] => 2. `false` under properties contributes 1 and sums with siblings => 2.

SIBLING INDEPENDENCE: every applicable keyword at the same level contributes independently. 1 vs {type:string,enum:[x,y],minimum:9,maxLength:0,multipleOf:7} => 4 (maxLength skipped for a non-string). {"a":[1,2]} vs {type,enum,required,minProperties,maxProperties,propertyNames} => 6. [1] vs {type,enum,const,minItems,maxItems,uniqueItems,items,contains} => 7 (uniqueItems passes).

Collapsing constructs coexist with siblings: "ab" vs {anyOf:[...],type:integer,minLength:9,not:{type:string},const:zz} => 5. {"a":1} vs {anyOf:[...],type:string,minLength:9,oneOf:[...]} => 3. A SATISFIED anyOf contributes 0 while its sibling required still fails => 1.

TYPE APPLICABILITY GATE: keywords whose target type does not match the instance yield 0 and are skipped silently. "s" vs a schema with properties/items/required/minItems/minProperties/additionalProperties:false/uniqueItems/contains/propertyNames/dependencies/minLength:9 => 1 (only minLength applies). Object keywords on an integer => 0. Array keywords on an object => 0.

LARGE COUNTS, no cap or dedupe: 30 wrong-typed items vs items{type:string} => 30; vs items{type:string,minimum:9} => 60; vs items{type:string,maxLength:0} => 30 (maxLength inapplicable to ints). 25 missing required => 25. 25 required + a 30-item array both failing in one run => 55. 100 sibling properties each failing => 100. [[1,1,1]x4] vs items>items{type:string,minimum:9,maxLength:0} => 24. 3 object props each holding [1,1,1] plus 2 required plus minProperties => 21.

KEYWORD ORDER IS IRRELEVANT to the count: {type,required,minProperties,properties} and its full reversal both => 4; nested {required,properties{required,properties}} in either order => 3; {minimum,type} == {type,minimum} => 2.

Collapse position matters: anyOf INSIDE items collapses per element ({x:{y:[1,2]}} => 2), anyOf ABOVE items collapses the whole subtree (=> 1), and anyOf plus sibling minItems plus sibling items => 4.
Mid-level collapse with pass-through ancestors: root required + properties.a.required + properties.a.anyOf[3-error subtree] => 3; the identical schema with allOf instead of anyOf => 5.

Deeply mixed: [{"a":[1]},{"a":[1]}] vs items>{properties:{a:{contains:{type:string},items:{type:string}}},required:[q]} => 6 (per element: contains 1 + item 1 + required 1). [1,2] vs items>{allOf:[{type:string},{not:{type:integer}}],oneOf:[{type:null}]} => 6 (per item: 2 allOf + 1 oneOf).
Recursive $ref terminated by the instance works fine: {"a":{"a":{"a":{"a":1}}}} vs {properties:{a:{$ref:'#'}},type:object} => 1 (only the innermost non-object fails).

Unknown keywords, $comment, unreferenced `definitions` subschemas, and draft-2019/2020 keywords (unevaluatedProperties, prefixItems) are all inert => 0. `format` is NOT validated (no format checker) => 0.

Exit code is 0 whenever a count is printed; on an unhandled exception stdout is EMPTY and exit is 1 (observed exceptions: RecursionError, jsonschema.exceptions._WrappedReferencingError PointerToNowhere/Unresolvable, and the unknown-`type` failure).
gotchas: $ref SUPPRESSES ALL SIBLING KEYWORDS in Draft7 (jsonschema builds `validators = [("$ref", ref)]` and ignores the rest). A naive JS implementation that evaluates siblings would over-count. Case: a={"a":1}, b={"$ref":"#/definitions/d","type":"array","required":["q"],"definitions":{"d":{"type":"string","minProperties":9}}} => 2, NOT 4.

`required` given a STRING instead of an array: Python iterates the string CHARACTER BY CHARACTER, producing one error per missing character. Case: a={"a":1}, b={"required":"abc"} => 2 ('a' present; 'b','c' missing). JS `for (const k of "abc")` happens to match, but `Array.isArray` guards or `schema.required.forEach` would not.

Type-applicability gating must be exact or counts drift: maxLength/minLength are skipped for non-strings, minimum/maximum/multipleOf for non-numbers, items/minItems/uniqueItems/contains/additionalItems for non-arrays, properties/required/minProperties/propertyNames/dependencies/additionalProperties for non-objects. Case: 30 integers vs {"items":{"type":"string","maxLength":0}} => 30, but vs {"items":{"type":"string","minimum":9}} => 60.

additionalItems is silently ignored when `items` is a schema rather than an array. Case: a=[1,2], b={"contains":{"type":"string"},"items":{"type":"string"},"uniqueItems":true,"additionalItems":false} => 3 (additionalItems contributes nothing).

Boolean `false` used as a per-item schema is NOT a collapsing construct: it fires once per index. Case: a=[1,2,3], b={"items":false} => 3; b={"items":[false,false]} => 2. Contrast additionalItems:false which is a single error ([1,2,3] with {"items":[{"type":"integer"}],"additionalItems":false} => 1).

additionalProperties:false, uniqueItems, additionalItems:false and contains each emit ONE error total, not one per offending property/duplicate/item. Cases: {"a":1,"b":2,"c":3} vs {"additionalProperties":false} => 1; [1x20] vs {"uniqueItems":true} => 1; [1..10] vs {"items":[],"additionalItems":false} => 1.

`not` inverts and DISCARDS the subtree: if the inner schema fails the result is 0 errors even though the inner schema would have produced several. Case: a={"a":1,"b":2,"c":3}, b={"not":{"properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}},"required":["q"]}} => 0.
The `if` subschema's own errors are never counted; only then/else propagate. Case: a={"a":1}, b={"if":{"type":"string"},"then":{"required":["q"]}} => 0.

A key matched by `properties` OR `patternProperties` is not 'additional', but properties AND patternProperties both validate it, and EVERY matching pattern applies. Cases: {"ab":1} vs {"properties":{"ab":{"type":"string"}},"patternProperties":{"^a":{"type":"null"}},"additionalProperties":false} => 2; {"ab":1} vs 3 overlapping patternProperties => 3.
Empty applicator arrays behave asymmetrically: {"anyOf":[]} => 1 and {"oneOf":[]} => 1, but {"allOf":[]} => 0 and {"enum":[]} => 1. Easy to get wrong with a naive `.some()`/`.every()`.
Nothing is deduped by message or by instance path. Case: a={}, b={"allOf":[{"required":["a"]},{"required":["a"]}]} => 2. A Set-of-errors implementation would return 1.
The same $ref target resolved from multiple places is counted once per resolution, not memoized-once. Case: a={"x":1,"y":{"x":1,"y":1}} with one definition reached 3 times, 2 errors each => 6.

Unresolvable or cyclic $ref THROWS instead of producing a count: {"$ref":"#"} and {"properties":{"a":{"$ref":"#/properties/a"}}} raise RecursionError; {"$ref":"#/definitions/missing"} raises _WrappedReferencingError PointerToNowhere; {"$ref":"http://example.com/x"} raises Unresolvable. JS would happily loop forever or return a count. Exit 1, stdout empty.
An unknown `type` value throws instead of being ignored: b={"type":"unknownType"} => exit 1 (UndefinedTypeCheck). A naive JS `types.includes(actual)` would return 1 error.

Python has finite recursion depth. Observed (not in the corpus, instances too large to store): a self-recursive $ref chain succeeds at instance depth 247 and raises RecursionError at depth 250; a schema of 400 nested `properties` levels succeeds while 600 raises RecursionError; plain json.loads handles depth 1100 fine when the schema is `true`. Node's stack limit is different, so extremely deep inputs will diverge.

Duplicate JSON object keys resolve LAST-WINS in both Python json.loads and JS JSON.parse, so counts agree: {"type":"string","type":"integer"} on 1 => 0 while {"type":"integer","type":"string"} on 1 => 1. Do not hand-roll a parser that keeps the first key.

Draft-2019/2020 keywords are inert in Draft7 (unevaluatedProperties, prefixItems => 0 errors), and `format` is never checked ("nope" vs {"format":"email"} => 0). Also inert: unknown keywords, $comment, and unreferenced entries in `definitions`.
exceptionCases: NOT in the case file (instances too large to store, but observed directly): self-recursive $ref {"properties":{"a":{"$ref":"#"}},"type":"object"} over an instance nested {"a":{"a":...}} 250 levels deep => RecursionError (247 levels still prints 1); a schema of 600 nested "properties" levels => RecursionError (400 levels prints 1).

rules: GLOBAL: every object keyword (properties, patternProperties, additionalProperties, required, minProperties, maxProperties, propertyNames, dependencies) first checks `is_type(instance,"object")` == "is a JSON object/dict" and returns silently otherwise. Arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null are all no-ops: `[1,2]` against a schema carrying ALL EIGHT object keywords set to fail => 0; the same schema against `{"a":1}` => 5.

GLOBAL: the printed number is the total count of individually-yielded errors, and it is exactly the SUM over keywords and over sub-errors; no dedup, no short-circuit. `{"a":1,"x":2,"BAD KEY":3}` vs properties(a:type string)+required[z]+minProperties5+maxProperties2+propertyNames(pattern ^[a-z]+$)+additionalProperties:false+dependencies{a:[q]} => 7.
required: ONE error per entry of the required list that is not a key of the instance. `{}` vs ["a","b","c"] => 3; `{"a":1,"b":2}` vs ["a","b","c","d"] => 2.
required duplicates are NOT deduped: `{}` vs ["a","a"] => 2; `{"a":1}` vs ["a","a"] => 0.
required: [] => 0. required entries are compared with Python `in` on the dict, i.e. exact key identity with no type coercion: `{"1":1}` vs required [1] => 1 error (int 1 is not the key "1").

required is iterated, not type-checked: a string value iterates its CHARACTERS (`{"required":"ab"}` on `{}` => 2, `"abc"` => 3, `"aa"` => 2), and an object value iterates its KEYS (`{"required":{"x":1,"y":2}}` on `{}` => 2).
required with a value that is not iterable raises (required:5 => exit 1); an unhashable entry raises (required:[["a"]] => exit 1, TypeError: unhashable type: 'list').
required only cares that the key exists: `{"a":null}` vs required ["a"] => 0.

properties: iterates schema.properties; a subschema is applied only if the key is PRESENT in the instance. Absent keys are never touched, so an invalid subschema for an absent key never raises (`{}` vs {"properties":{"a":5}} => 0, while `{"a":5}` vs the same => exit 1).

properties: every sub-error of every failing property is a separate top-level error. `{"a":1,"b":2}` vs a/b both type:string => 2; `{"a":1}` vs {"a":{"type":"string","minimum":5}} => 2; `{"a":{"b":1}}` vs properties.a={properties:{b:{type:string}},required:[z,y]} => 3.
properties subschema `false` => 1 error when key present, 0 when absent; `true` => 0.

patternProperties: for EACH pattern that matches a key (Python `re.search`, i.e. UNANCHORED substring search), the key's value is validated; the same key can be hit by several patterns and every error counts. `{"aa":1}` vs {"^a":{type:string},"a$":{type:string}} => 2; `{"bab":1}` vs {"a":{type:string}} => 1; `{"a":1,"ab":2}` vs {"^a$":{type:string},"^a":{maximum:0}} => 3.

patternProperties: an empty pattern "" matches every key (`{"a":1,"b":2}` vs {"":{type:string}} => 2). Non-matching keys are ignored, so an invalid subschema behind a non-matching pattern never raises ({"patternProperties":{"a":5}} on `{"b":1}` => 0, on `{"a":1}` => exit 1). An invalid regex raises (pattern "[" => exit 1, re.error).

additionalProperties: 'additional' = instance keys that are (a) not literally a key of schema.properties AND (b) not matched by the SINGLE regex formed by `"|".join(schema.patternProperties keys)` searched unanchored. Whether a declared property or a matching pattern actually VALIDATES is irrelevant: `{"a":"x"}` vs {properties:{a:{type:number}},additionalProperties:false} => 1 (properties error only); `{"a":1}` vs {properties:{a:false},additionalProperties:false} => 1.
additionalProperties === false yields EXACTLY ONE error no matter how many extras: 2 extras => 1, 5 extras => 1, 0 extras => 0.

additionalProperties as an OBJECT schema is applied per extra key and yields the full per-extra error count: {"type":"string"} on 2 non-string extras => 2; {"type":"string","maximum":0} on 2 extras => 4; {"required":["z","w"]} on `{"x":{},"y":{}}` => 4; {"properties":{"n":{"type":"string"}}} on `{"x":{"n":1},"y":{"n":2}}` => 2; `{}` => 0.

additionalProperties dispatch is Python-truthiness based, NOT schema-type based: only a dict is treated as a schema; otherwise, FALSY values ([] , 0, null, false) each produce the single 'not allowed' error when extras exist, and TRUTHY non-dict values (true, 1, "nope", [1,2]) produce 0 errors. Observed: aP [] => 1, aP 0 => 1, aP null => 1, aP true => 0, aP 1 => 0, aP "nope" => 0, aP [1,2] => 0.

additionalProperties + properties + patternProperties: `{"a":1,"bb":2,"c":3,"d":4}` vs {properties:{a:{}},patternProperties:{"^b":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 1; with additionalProperties {"type":"string"} => 2 (only c and d). `{"x":1}` vs {properties:{},additionalProperties:false} => 1.

propertyNames: descends into the subschema once PER KEY, with the key STRING as the instance; N bad names => N errors, and multiple keyword failures on one name each count. `{"x":1,"y":2}` vs propertyNames:false => 2; vs propertyNames:true => 0; `{}` vs propertyNames:false => 0; `{"abc":1,"de":2}` vs {maxLength:2} => 1; `{"ab":1}` vs {minLength:5,pattern:"^y"} => 2; `{"x":1}` vs {type:"number"} => 1; vs {not:{type:"string"}} => 1; vs {required:["z"]} => 0 (object keywords are inert on a string).
propertyNames with a non-schema value raises only if the object is non-empty ({"propertyNames":5} on `{"x":1}` => exit 1).
dependencies (draft7 legacy, both forms in one keyword): the dependency is only considered if its KEY is present in the instance (`{}` vs {"a":["b","c"]} => 0; `{}` vs {"a":false} => 0).

dependencies ARRAY form: one error per listed name missing from the instance, duplicates counted twice, no coercion. {"a":["b","c"]} on `{"a":1}` => 2; {"a":["b","b"]} => 2; {"a":[]} => 0; {"a":["b"]} on `{"a":1,"b":2}` => 0; {"a":[1]} on `{"1":1,"a":2}` => 1; {"a":[true]} on `{"a":1}` => 1; {"a":[["b"]]} => exit 1 (unhashable).

dependencies SCHEMA form (any non-array value): the subschema is validated against the WHOLE instance object and all sub-errors count. {"a":{"required":["x","y"]}} on `{"a":1}` => 2; {"a":{"minProperties":3,"maxProperties":0}} => 2; {"a":{"properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}}}} => 1; {"a":false} => 1; {"a":true} => 0; {"a":{}} => 0. Multiple triggered dependency keys sum: {"a":["c"],"b":["d"]} on `{"a":1,"b":2}` => 2.

dependencies with a scalar non-array value (string/number) raises when the key is present: {"a":"b"} => exit 1 (AttributeError 'str' has no attribute 'get'), {"a":5} => exit 1. dependencies itself not an object => exit 1. dependencies {} => 0.

minProperties/maxProperties: at most ONE error each, computed as `len(instance) < min` / `len(instance) > max` on the number of own keys. `{}` vs min 1 => 1; 2 keys vs min 5 => 1 (not 3); min 0 => 0; min -1 => (dropped) ; max 0 on 1 key => 1; max -1 on `{}` => 1; both failing => 2. Nested keys are not counted (`{"a":{"b":{"c":1}}}` vs {maxProperties:1,properties:{a:{maxProperties:0}}} => 1).

minProperties/maxProperties accept non-integers: floats compare numerically (2 keys vs min 2.5 => 1, vs min 2.0 => 0; 2 keys vs max 1.5 => 1) and JSON booleans act as 1/0 (`{}` vs min true => 1, `{"a":1}` vs min true => 0, vs min false => 0). 1e400 parses to +inf (`{"a":1}` vs min 1e400 => 1).

minProperties/maxProperties with a non-number (string/null) raises ONLY for object instances, because the is_type check short-circuits first: {"minProperties":"2"} on `{}` => exit 1 but on `[]` => 0; {"maxProperties":null} on `{"a":1}` => exit 1.

Duplicate keys in the instance JSON: LAST occurrence wins and the object has one key. `{"a":"x","a":1}` vs properties.a.type=string => 1; `{"a":1,"a":"x"}` vs the same => 0; `{"a":1,"a":2}` vs minProperties 2 => 1; vs maxProperties 1 => 0. Duplicate keys in the SCHEMA JSON also last-wins: {"required":["a"],"required":["b","c"]} on `{}` => 2.
Key comparison is exact and case-sensitive: `{"A":1,"a":2}` vs {properties:{a:{type:string}},additionalProperties:false} => 2 (a fails type, A is additional).

Draft7 dialect is forced: `dependentRequired` and `dependentSchemas` are UNKNOWN keywords and yield 0 even when they would fail, including when the schema declares "$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema". Miscased/unknown keywords (minproperties, Required, unknownKeyword) are ignored => 0.

properties and patternProperties are independent and both apply to the same key: `{"ab":"x"}` vs {patternProperties:{"^a":{type:string}},properties:{ab:{type:number}}} => 1; `{"a":1,"b":2}` vs {properties:{a:string,b:string},patternProperties:{"^":{type:string}},additionalProperties:false,propertyNames:{minLength:3}} => 6 (2 properties + 2 patternProperties + 0 additional + 2 names).

Nested object keywords behave identically at depth: `{"o":{"x":1,"y":2}}` vs properties.o.additionalProperties=false => 1; vs properties.o.propertyNames=false => 2; `{"o":{"x":1}}` vs properties.o={required:[p,q],additionalProperties:false,propertyNames:{maxLength:0}} => 4.
gotchas: additionalProperties builds ONE regex by `"|".join(patternProperties.keys())` and calls re.search on it, instead of testing each pattern separately. Three observable consequences: (1) a lone empty pattern makes the joined string "" which is FALSY, so the pattern check is skipped entirely and every key becomes additional -- `{"a":1,"b":2}` vs {patternProperties:{"":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 1; (2) adding any other pattern makes it truthy and the empty alternative then matches everything -- {patternProperties:{"^a":{},"":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 0; (3) group numbering shifts, so a backreference can stop matching once joined -- `{"aa":1}` vs {patternProperties:{"(x)y":{},"(a)\\1":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 1, while the same backref pattern alone gives {patternProperties:{"(a)\\1":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 0.

additionalProperties dispatch uses Python truthiness on non-dict values, which JS `!value` matches for 0/null/false/"" but NOT for arrays: `[]` is FALSY in Python and yields the single 'additional properties not allowed' error, while JS `![]` is false. Observed: {"additionalProperties":[]} on `{"x":1}` => 1, {"additionalProperties":[1,2]} => 0. So the JS rule must be: dict->schema; else `isFalsy = v===false||v===null||v===0||v===""||(Array.isArray(v)&&v.length===0)`.

required / dependencies membership uses Python `in` on a dict, which does NOT coerce: required [1] against `{"1":1}` => 1 error, and dependencies {"a":[1]} against `{"1":1,"a":2}` => 1 error. Naive JS `Object.hasOwn(obj, 1)` or `obj[1]` stringifies the key to "1" and would report 0. Only compare when the entry is `typeof === "string"`; any non-string entry (number, boolean, null) is always 'missing'. Unhashable entries (arrays/objects) throw instead: required [["a"]] => exit 1, dependencies {"a":[["b"]]} => exit 1.

required is duck-typed as an iterable, so a JSON STRING iterates code points and a JSON OBJECT iterates keys: {"required":"ab"} on `{}` => 2, {"required":"abc"} => 3, {"required":{"x":1,"y":2}} => 2. JS `for (const p of required)` happens to match for strings but you must special-case plain objects (iterate keys) and throw for numbers ({"required":5} => exit 1).

Property-name string length is measured in Unicode CODE POINTS (Python len), not UTF-16 units. Key U+1D552 (surrogate pair) vs {"propertyNames":{"maxLength":1}} => 0 and vs {"minLength":2} => 1; key U+1D552 + "b" vs {"maxLength":2} => 0. Naive JS `name.length` gives 2 and 3 and would flip all three. Use [...name].length.

Python `$` matches immediately before a trailing newline, so a key ending in 
 still matches an anchored pattern. `{"a
":1}` vs {"propertyNames":{"pattern":"^a$"}} => 0 (JS /^a$/ would fail => 1); the same key vs {"patternProperties":{"^a$":false}} => 1 error and vs {patternProperties:{"^a$":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 0 (so JS would wrongly call it additional). Emulate by treating `$` as `(?=
?$)` / rewriting to /^a$/m-like behavior only for a single trailing newline.

Python inline regex flags are supported and JS RegExp rejects them outright (SyntaxError): {"patternProperties":{"(?i)^a":{...}}} matched key "A" => 1 error, and {"propertyNames":{"pattern":"(?m)^b"}} matched key "a\nb" => 0 errors. Also Python-only syntax that JS does not accept: \A and \Z anchors ({"patternProperties":{"a\\Z":{...}}} on `{"a":1}` => 1; {"propertyNames":{"pattern":"\\Aa\\Z"}} on `{"a":1}` => 0) and named groups (?P<n>...) ({"patternProperties":{"(?P<n>b)":{...}}} on `{"abc":1}` => 1). A JS port must translate (?i)->i flag, (?m)->m flag, \A->^, \Z->$, (?P<x>->(?<x>.

Python 3 \d, \w, \s are Unicode-aware by default; JS \d/\w are ASCII-only. Key U+0663 (Arabic-Indic digit three) vs {"patternProperties":{"\\d":false}} => 1 error; key U+00E9 vs {"patternProperties":{"\\w":false}} => 1 error and vs {"\\W":false} => 0 errors. Naive JS gives the opposite for all three.

All regex matching is re.search (UNANCHORED) in patternProperties, propertyNames' `pattern`, and the additionalProperties join. `{"bab":1}` vs {patternProperties:{"a":{type:string}}} => 1; `{"abc":1}` vs {propertyNames:{pattern:"b"}} => 0; `{"ab":1}` vs {patternProperties:{"b":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 0. JS must use regex.test (no ^...$ wrapping).

minProperties/maxProperties are raw `<`/`>` comparisons, so JSON booleans behave as 1/0 (`{}` vs {"minProperties":true} => 1, `{"a":1}` vs {"minProperties":true} => 0, vs {"minProperties":false} => 0) and non-numbers THROW -- but only after the is_type(object) guard: {"minProperties":"2"} on `{}` => exit 1 while on `[]` => 0. JS `1 < "2"` silently coerces and `1 > null` is true, so both would wrongly return counts.

Malformed subschemas raise only when actually reached, so laziness is observable and must be reproduced: {"properties":{"a":5}} => exit 1 on `{"a":5}` but 0 on `{}`; {"patternProperties":{"a":5}} => exit 1 on `{"a":1}` but 0 on `{"b":1}`; {"propertyNames":5} => exit 1 on `{"x":1}`; an invalid regex {"patternProperties":{"[":{}}} => exit 1. A JS port that pre-compiles/pre-validates the whole schema would throw on cases the reference answers 0 for.

additionalProperties' 'is it declared?' test is `property not in schema.get("properties", {})`, i.e. membership on whatever properties happens to be -- but a non-dict properties makes the properties keyword itself throw first, so {"properties":["a"],"additionalProperties":false} => exit 1 and {"patternProperties":5,"additionalProperties":false} => exit 1. Errors are never partially printed: list(iter_errors) consumes the whole generator, so any raise anywhere means empty stdout and exit 1 even if other keywords already produced errors.

Draft7Validator is hard-coded, so 2019-09/2020-12 replacements must NOT be implemented: {"dependentRequired":{"a":["b"]}} on `{"a":1}` => 0, {"dependentSchemas":{"a":false}} => 0, and an explicit "$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema" does not change that => 0.

Duplicate keys in the raw instance/schema JSON follow last-wins (identical to JS JSON.parse) and collapse the key count: `{"a":"x","a":1}` vs properties.a.type=string => 1 while `{"a":1,"a":"x"}` => 0, and `{"a":1,"a":2}` vs minProperties 2 => 1. A hand-rolled parser that keeps both or first-wins would diverge.

rules: ENGINE: `pattern` is evaluated as Python `re.search(schema_pattern, instance)` -> UNANCHORED, and yields AT MOST 1 error. instance "abc": pattern "b"=>0, "^b"=>1, "b$"=>1, "^abc$"=>0, ""=>0.

LAZY COMPILE: `pattern` is only touched when the instance is a JSON string. instance 123 or {"x":1} with pattern "^a$" => 0; instance 5 with the INVALID pattern "[" => 0 (no exception). Same for patternProperties on a non-object, and for a string instance carrying a bogus patternProperties: {"pattern":"b","patternProperties":{"[":{}}} vs "abc" => 0.

NON-STRING pattern VALUE => exception: {"pattern":5} and {"pattern":null} => TypeError 'first argument must be string or compiled pattern'; {"pattern":["b"]} => TypeError 'unhashable type: list'. All exit 1, empty stdout.

NO FLAGS are passed by jsonschema: matching is case-SENSITIVE, non-MULTILINE, non-DOTALL by default ("ABC" vs "^abc$" => 1). Flags are only obtainable via inline (?imsxau) groups at the very start of the pattern.

\d = Unicode category Nd. Matches: U+0663 Arabic-Indic 3 =>0, U+FF11 fullwidth 1 =>0, U+0F20 Tibetan 0 =>0. Does NOT match U+00B2 (No) =>1, U+2160 (Nl) =>1. \D is the exact complement (U+0663 vs "^\\D$" => 1). Inside a class it is identical: U+0663 vs "^[\\d]$" => 0, but "^[0-9]$" => 1.

\w = Unicode word chars (letters of all categories + Nd/No/Nl + '_'). Matches U+0663=>0, U+00E9=>0, U+00B2=>0, U+00BD=>0, U+2160=>0, U+00B5=>0, U+4E2D=>0, U+02B0=>0, "_"=>0. Does NOT match combining marks: U+0301 alone =>1 and "é" vs "^\\w+$" =>1; emoji U+1F600 =>1; "-" =>1.

\s = Python Unicode whitespace: matches U+00A0=>0, U+3000=>0, U+000B=>0, U+001C=>0, U+001D=>0, U+001F=>0, U+0085=>0, U+2028=>0, U+2029=>0. Does NOT match U+001B=>1, U+FEFF=>1, U+200B=>1. \S is the exact complement (U+001C vs "^\\S$"=>1, U+FEFF vs "^\\S$"=>0). Identical inside a class (U+001C vs "^[\\s]$"=>0).
WORD BOUNDARY \b/\B are Unicode-aware because \w is: "éx" vs "\\bx" => 1 and vs "\\Bx" => 0; "٣x" vs "\\bx" => 1. ASCII baseline: "foo bar" vs "\\bbar\\b" => 0, "foobar" vs "\\bbar" => 1.

INLINE FLAG SUPPORT: (?a) forces ASCII (U+0663 vs "(?a)^\\d$" => 1; U+00E9 vs "(?a)^\\w$" => 1). (?u) is a no-op. (?i)(?s) as two separate groups at the start is fine ("abc" vs "(?i)(?s)^A.C$" => 0) as is combined "(?is)^A.C$" => 0. (?L) with a str pattern is an exception.

GLOBAL INLINE FLAGS MUST BE AT POSITION 0: "a(?i)b", "^(?i)abc$", "((?i)a)" all => exception (re.error: global flags not at the start of the expression); "(?i)^a(?-i)b$" => exception (missing : at position 10). SCOPED flag groups work anywhere: "aB" vs "^a(?i:b)$" => 0; "AB" vs "(?i)^a(?-i:b)$" => 1.

CODE POINTS, NOT UTF-16 UNITS: an astral char is ONE character. "😀" vs "^.$" => 0 and vs "^..$" => 1; "a😀b" vs "^a.b$" => 0; vs "^[\\u0000-\\uffff]$" => 1. A lone surrogate survives json.loads and counts as 1 char: "\ud800" vs "^.$" => 0.

PYTHON-ONLY SYNTAX THAT WORKS (all 0 errors when matching): (?P<n>a) ; (?P<n>a)(?P=n) vs "aa" ; (?P<n>a)\\1 vs "aa" ; (?#comment)a ; "(?x) a  b " vs "ab" ; octal \\101 vs "A" ; \\0 vs U+0000 ; \\N{LATIN SMALL LETTER A} vs "a" ; possessive "^a++$" vs "aa" ; atomic "^(?>a)$" vs "a" ; conditional "^(a)?(?(1)b|c)$" vs "ab"=>0 and vs "c"=>0.

CHARACTER-CLASS EDGE CASES: "[]" and "[^]" are EXCEPTIONS (unterminated character set). "^[]]$" vs "]" => 0 (the first ] after [ or [^ is a literal member) and "^[^]]$" vs "a" => 0. "[[:alpha:]]" is NOT a POSIX class: it is the class [[:alph] followed by a literal ] -> vs "a" => 1, vs "a]" => 0. Bad ranges are exceptions: "[a-\\d]", "[z-a]", "[\\w-a]".

BRACE QUANTIFIERS: "{,n}" means "{0,n}": "^a{,3}$" vs ""=>0, "aaa"=>0, "aaaa"=>1, "a{,3}"=>1. "{,}" means "{0,}": "^a{,}$" vs ""=>0, "a"=>0, "a{,}"=>1. Unparsable brace forms are LITERAL: "^a{}$" vs "a{}"=>0 / vs "a"=>1; "^a{1,2,3}$" vs "a{1,2,3}"=>0. "a{2,1}" is an exception (min repeat greater than max repeat).
BACKREFERENCES: "\\1" with no group => exception (invalid group reference 1) even when the instance is ""; "\\8" => exception (invalid group reference 8).

BAD ESCAPES (exception) are exactly the unknown ASCII-letter escapes: \\z, \\e, \\p (so \\p{L} is fatal), \\k (so \\k<n> is fatal), \\Q, and a trailing lone backslash "a\\" (bad escape (end of pattern)). Escapes of NON-alphanumerics are fine: "^\\-$" vs "-"=>0, "^[\\-]$"=>0, "^[\\/]$" vs "/"=>0, "^a\\\\$" vs a literal backslash => 0. "\\x{61}" => exception (incomplete escape \x).

LOOKAROUND: lookbehind must be FIXED WIDTH. "(?<=a)b" vs "ab" => 0, but "(?<=a+)b" and "(?<=aa|b)b" => exception (look-behind requires fixed-width pattern). "^(?<=a)b$" vs "ab" => 1 (the ^ pins position 0 so the lookbehind cannot succeed).
JS-STYLE CONSTRUCTS ARE FATAL: "(?<n>a)" => exception (unknown extension ?<n); "\\k<n>" => exception.

IGNORECASE (only reachable via (?i)) uses Python's SIMPLE case folding plus a reverse-equivalence table, and is fully Unicode-aware. Confirmed equivalence classes (all => 0): k/K/U+212A KELVIN; s/S/U+017F LONG S; i/I/U+0131 DOTLESS I/U+0130 DOTTED CAPITAL I (all four interchangeable); U+03C3/U+03C2/U+03A3 sigma; U+00E5/U+212B ANGSTROM; U+03C9/U+2126 OHM; U+00B5 MICRO/U+03BC GREEK MU; U+00DF/U+1E9E SHARP S; U+03B9/U+0345 YPOGEGRAMMENI; U+00E9/U+00C9. NOT full casefolding: U+00DF vs "(?i)^ss$" => 1 and "SS" vs "(?i)^ß$" => 1. No compatibility folding: U+FF21 vs "(?i)^a$" => 1. Without (?i): U+212A vs "^k$" => 1, U+00B5 vs "^μ$" => 1.
IGNORECASE APPLIES INSIDE CLASSES AND RANGES: U+212A vs "(?i)^[k]$" => 0; U+212A, U+017F, U+0131, U+0130 all vs "(?i)^[a-z]$" => 0; the negated form excludes them: U+212A vs "(?i)^[^a-z]$" => 1.

patternProperties KEY MATCHING IS re.search (unanchored) with all the same Python semantics: {"xay":1} vs patternProperties {"a":{type:string}} => 1, vs {"^a":...} => 0; empty pattern "" and "^$" both match key "" => 1 each; key "a\nb" vs "^b$" => 0 but vs "(?m)^b$" => 1; key "a\n" vs "a$" => 1 (trailing-newline quirk); key "٣" vs "\\d" => 1.

patternProperties ERROR COUNT = (number of (pattern, key) pairs where re.search hits AND the subschema fails), each independent: 2 patterns matching 1 key => 2 ({"xa":1} vs {"a":str,"^x":str} => 2; {"a":1} vs {"a":str,"^a$":bool} => 2); 1 pattern matching 2 keys => 2 ({"a":1,"b":2} vs {".":str} => 2; {"a":1,"aa":2} vs {"a":str} => 2); multiple regex hits within ONE key still count once ({"aa":1} vs {"a":str} => 1). Nested subschema errors collapse into 1 top-level error ({"a":{"b":1}} vs patternProperties.a.patternProperties.b.type=string => 1).

patternProperties REGEXES ARE COMPILED PER PROPERTY, so an invalid one is only fatal if the instance is an object with at least one key: {} vs {"patternProperties":{"[":{}}} => 0, 5 => 0, but {"x":1} => exception. An earlier matching valid pattern does not shield a later invalid one: {"x":1} vs {"^x":{type:string},"[":{}} => exception.

additionalProperties EXCLUSION USES THE SAME re.search: {"ab":1,"b":2} vs {patternProperties:{"^a":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 1 (only "b"); {"xa":1} vs {patternProperties:{"a":{}},additionalProperties:false} => 0 (unanchored hit consumes the key); with additionalProperties as a schema {type:string} the count is also 1.
properties AND patternProperties BOTH RUN INDEPENDENTLY: {"a":true} vs {properties:{a:{type:string}}, patternProperties:{"^a":{type:number}}} => 2.

TOP-LEVEL COUNTING AROUND pattern: pattern contributes exactly one error and sums with sibling keywords: {"pattern":"^a$","minLength":5} vs "X" => 2; {"pattern":"^b$","maxLength":2,"enum":["q"]} vs "aaa" => 3. Applicators: allOf yields one top-level error per failing branch ({allOf:[{pattern:"^x"},{pattern:"y$"}]} vs "abc" => 2), while anyOf, oneOf and not each collapse to 1 ({anyOf:[...]} => 1, {oneOf:[{pattern:"^a"},{pattern:"c$"}]} with both matching => 1, {not:{pattern:"b"}} vs "abc" => 1).

pattern ALSO REACHABLE VIA propertyNames AND items with the same 1-error-per-application rule: {"1":1} vs {propertyNames:{pattern:"^[a-z]+$"}} => 1; ["ab"] vs {items:{pattern:"^b"}} => 1. Their regexes are likewise lazily compiled: [] vs {items:{pattern:"["}} => 0, {} vs {propertyNames:{pattern:"["}} => 0, but {"a":1} vs {propertyNames:{pattern:"["}} => exception.

re.error PROPAGATES OUT OF EVERYTHING - it is not caught and converted to a validation error: {"type":"number","pattern":"["} vs "abc" => exception (the failing type keyword does not prevent it); {"anyOf":[{"pattern":"["}]} vs "abc" => exception. Exit code is 1 with EMPTY stdout in all such cases.

DUPLICATE JSON KEYS: last occurrence wins, in both schema and instance (Python json.loads and JS JSON.parse agree). {"patternProperties":{"a":{type:string},"a":{type:number}}} vs {"a":"x"} => 1; {"x":1,"x":"s"} vs {patternProperties:{"x":{type:string}}} => 0.

`[]` and `[^]` are Python re.error (unterminated character set) => EXIT 1; in JS `[]` never matches and `[^]` matches anything. And `[]]`/`[^]]` mean the opposite thing: "]" vs "^[]]$" => 0 and "a" vs "^[^]]$" => 0, whereas JS reads them as empty-class-plus-literal-] / any-plus-literal-] and would give 1 and 1.

Variable-width lookbehind is a fatal Python error but perfectly legal in JS: "(?<=a+)b" and "(?<=aa|b)b" => EXIT 1 (look-behind requires fixed-width pattern), where JS would report 0.

IGNORECASE is Unicode simple-casefold PLUS reverse-mapping, matching NEITHER JS mode. Python: U+212A vs "(?i)^k$" => 0, U+017F vs "(?i)^s$" => 0, U+0131 and U+0130 vs "(?i)^i$" => 0, U+00B5 vs "(?i)^μ$" => 0, U+1E9E vs "(?i)^ß$" => 0, U+0345 vs "(?i)^ι$" => 0, and all of these also work inside ranges ("(?i)^[a-z]$" matches U+212A/U+017F/U+0131/U+0130). `[[:alpha:]]` is not a POSIX class in either language, but confirm the exact reading: it is the class [[:alph] followed by a LITERAL ]. "a" => 1, "a]" => 0.

A JS port that does `new RegExp(5)` would happily match "5" instead.

Nested failures collapse to one top-level error ({"a":{"b":1}} => 1).
